newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal's Socialists seek to end internal row.
newsitem.headline: Portugal's Socialists seek to end internal row.

text.p: Portugal's ruling Socialists were seeking on Wednesday to end to an embarrassing internal row over constitutional reform after party deputies spurned an accord reached with the main opposition.

A meeting of the party's parliamentary deputies rejected the pact, which would include a possible cut in the number of parliamentarians and give the vote to Portuguese living abroad, at a late night session on Tuesday.
Just hours after sealing the deal with the main opposition Social Democrats, Socialist leader in parliament Jorge Lacao backtracked and said it amounted to no more than a set of proposals.

The party's national committee, its top policy-making body, was due to meet later on Wednesday to seek a way out of the impasse which threatens to pit Socialist Prime Minister Antonio Guterres against a significant sector of his own party for the second time in a week.
Parliament narrowly rejected a bid last Thursday to liberalise Portugal's restrictive abortion laws after a handful of Socialists sided with the opposition.

Guterres, a practising Roman Catholic, angered Socialist supporters of abortion reform by announcing his personal opposition to change in a move which probably tipped the parliamentary balance, political analysts said.

Complex negotiations between the ruling party and the Social Democrats on a series of reforms to the constitution, which had dragged on for months, appeared concluded on Tuesday when leaders of both parties announced that only minor details remained to be settled.

The accord would open the way to changing the country's near-pure proportional representation system by allowing the introduction of British-style, single member constituencies while retaining some proportional element.
Obligatory military service would be abolished and Portuguese emigrants would be given the right to vote in presidential elections provided they met certain conditions.

"This is a very good agreement. The Socialists have put the good of the country above party political interests," said Social Democrat leader Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa whose party has long demanded the right of emigrants to vote.

But Socialist deputies, many claiming that they had not been consulted about the deal, dug in their heels over the emigrant vote and the notion of a cut in the number of parliamentarians from the present 230.
"Such changes can only be agreed after consulting the parliamentary party," warned Socialist deputy Ricardo Castanheira.
